notes.front: What is SAML single sign-on (SAML SSO) on GitHub Enterprise Cloud?
notes.back: An additional access restriction: members with their own GitHub.com accounts must also authenticate through the company’s SAML identity provider.
notes.explanation: It gives organization and enterprise owners a way to control and secure access to organization resources such as repositories, issues and pull requests.
notes.example: Like a building pass checked at the office door, on top of the house key each employee already carries.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About SAML for enterprise IAM”, “About SAML SSO for your enterprise”
notes.evidence: If your enterprise members manage their own user accounts on GitHub.com, you can configure SAML authentication as an additional access restriction for your enterprise or organization. Single sign-on (SSO) gives organization owners and enterprise owners a way to control and secure access to organization resources like repositories, issues, and pull requests.

notes.front: What does an SSH certificate authority (SSH CA) let an enterprise do?
notes.back: Let members of its organizations access those organizations’ repositories with SSH certificates that the enterprise provides.
notes.explanation: You can also require members to use SSH certificates to access organization resources.
notes.example: Like a company that stamps its own time-limited visitor badges, instead of each visitor bringing an unchecked key.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for security settings in your enterprise”, “Managing SSH certificate authorities for your enterprise”
notes.evidence: You can use a SSH certificate authority (CA) to allow members of any organization owned by your enterprise to access that organization's repositories using SSH certificates you provide.

notes.front: What is a linked external identity?
notes.back: The link GitHub records, in an organization or enterprise, between your GitHub personal account and the IdP identity you signed in with.
notes.explanation: GitHub uses it to validate your organization membership and, depending on setup, to work out which organizations and teams you belong to.
notes.example: Like a staff directory entry that ties your personal phone number to your employee record.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About authentication with single sign-on”, “Linked external identities”
notes.evidence: When you authenticate with your IdP account and return to GitHub, GitHub will record a link in the organization or enterprise between your GitHub personal account and the external identity you signed into.

notes.front: What is SSO authorization of a token or SSH key?
notes.back: Authorizing a personal access token or SSH key for use with an organization that uses or enforces SSO.
notes.explanation: Without it, a token or key cannot be used with the organization, whether the credential is new or existing.
notes.example: Like registering your car’s number plate with an office car park before the barrier will lift for it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About authentication with single sign-on”, “Authorizing personal access tokens and SSH keys with SSO”
notes.evidence: To use a new or existing personal access token or SSH key with an organization that uses or enforces SSO, you will need to authorize the token or authorize the SSH key for use with the organization.

notes.front: What are an enterprise account’s single sign-on recovery codes for?
notes.back: Signing in and accessing the enterprise on GitHub when the identity provider is unavailable.
notes.explanation: Without them, an IdP outage would leave administrators unable to reach the enterprise, so GitHub Docs says you should download them.
notes.example: Like a spare key kept in a safe for the day the electronic door lock fails.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Downloading your enterprise account’s single sign-on recovery codes”
notes.evidence: To ensure that you can access GitHub if your identity provider (IdP) is unavailable, you should download your enterprise account's single sign-on (SSO) recovery codes. In the event that your IdP is unavailable, you can use a recovery code to sign in and access your enterprise on GitHub.

notes.front: In an enterprise with managed users, what is OpenID Connect (OIDC) used for?
notes.back: Managing authentication for the enterprise: an alternative to SAML for single sign-on with the IdP.
notes.explanation: With Enterprise Managed Users the IdP authenticates every member, and OIDC is one way to connect it; enabling it is a one-click setup.
notes.example: Like switching a building’s entry system to a newer badge standard, while the same security desk still checks everyone.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring OIDC for Enterprise Managed Users”, “About OIDC for Enterprise Managed Users”
notes.evidence: With Enterprise Managed Users, your enterprise uses your identity provider (IdP) to authenticate all members. You can use OpenID Connect (OIDC) to manage authentication for your enterprise with managed users. Enabling OIDC SSO is a one-click setup process with certificates managed by GitHub and your IdP.

notes.front: With OIDC SSO, what does GitHub use the IdP’s Conditional Access Policy (CAP) for?
notes.back: Its IP conditions validate interactions with GitHub: web use, IP address changes, and each authentication with a user’s token or SSH key.
notes.explanation: GitHub applies the policy automatically once the enterprise uses OIDC SSO, so the IdP’s own conditions govern GitHub access too.
notes.example: Like a rule that office systems only open from the company network, enforced by the same desk that issues badges.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring OIDC for Enterprise Managed Users”, “About OIDC for Enterprise Managed Users”
notes.evidence: When your enterprise uses OIDC SSO, GitHub will automatically use your IdP's conditional access policy (CAP) IP conditions to validate interactions with GitHub when members use the web UI or change IP addresses, and for each authentication with a personal access token or SSH key associated with a user account.

notes.front: Which 2FA methods does GitHub count as secure two-factor methods?
notes.back: Passkeys, security keys, authenticator apps and the GitHub mobile app.
notes.explanation: An organization can require these exclusively, alongside requiring 2FA itself, for members, billing managers and outside collaborators.
notes.example: Like a bank that accepts a hardware token or its own app for approvals, but no longer a code sent by text message.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Requiring two-factor authentication in your organization”, “Requiring secure methods of two-factor authentication in your organization”
notes.evidence: Alongside requiring two-factor authentication, you can require that organization members, billing managers, and outside collaborators use secure methods of 2FA exclusively. Secure two-factor methods are passkeys, security keys, authenticator apps, and the GitHub mobile app.

notes.front: What is mandatory 2FA on GitHub.com?
notes.back: GitHub’s own requirement that accounts selected as contributors enable 2FA.
notes.explanation: An account is selected when it has taken an action on GitHub that shows it is a contributor.
notes.example: Like a bank requiring stronger sign-in only for customers who make payments, whatever their employer demands.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About mandatory two-factor authentication”, “About eligibility for mandatory 2FA”
notes.evidence: Your account is selected for mandatory 2FA if you have taken some action on GitHub that shows you are a contributor.

notes.front: With authentication solely through GitHub.com, who creates and manages each member’s account?
notes.back: Each person creates and manages their own personal account on GitHub.com.
notes.explanation: Once the enterprise grants that account access, the member reaches enterprise resources simply by signing in to GitHub.com.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Identity and access management fundamentals”, “Authentication through GitHub.com”
notes.evidence: With authentication solely through GitHub.com, each person you want to grant access to your enterprise must create and manage a personal account on GitHub.com. After you grant access to your enterprise, the member can access your enterprise's resources after signing into the account on GitHub.com.

notes.front: With the additional SAML access restriction, what must a member authenticate to before reaching enterprise resources?
notes.back: Both their GitHub.com account and an account on the SAML identity provider.
notes.explanation: The member still has a personal account on GitHub.com; the IdP check is added on top of it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Identity and access management fundamentals”, “Authentication through GitHub.com with additional SAML access restriction”
notes.evidence: After you grant access to your enterprise, the member can access your enterprise's resources only after authenticating successfully for both the account on GitHub.com and for an account on your SAML identity provider (IdP).

notes.front: With Enterprise Managed Users and federation, whose account does each member sign in to?
notes.back: An account the enterprise creates and manages through its IdP.
notes.explanation: GitHub Docs presents this option for when you need more control of members’ accounts; contributions outside the enterprise are restricted.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Identity and access management fundamentals”, “Authentication with Enterprise Managed Users and federation”
notes.evidence: If you need more control of the accounts for your enterprise members on GitHub, you can use Enterprise Managed Users. With Enterprise Managed Users, you provision and manage accounts for your enterprise members on GitHub using your IdP. Each member signs into an account that you create, and your enterprise manages the account.

notes.front: A firm lets developers use the GitHub.com accounts they already have, but wants every access to its enterprise’s resources also checked against its corporate IdP. Which authentication option fits?
notes.back: A) Authentication through GitHub.com with additional SAML access restriction
notes.explanation: Members keep their personal accounts but reach resources only after authenticating to both GitHub.com and the SAML IdP.
notes.choices:
A) Authentication through GitHub.com with additional SAML access restriction
B) Authentication solely through GitHub.com
C) Enterprise Managed Users with federation
D) GitHub Enterprise Server with built-in authentication
notes.choicesExplained: B) This option has no IdP check. C) With Enterprise Managed Users people cannot keep their own accounts; the enterprise creates them. D) GHES is a self-hosted deployment, and built-in authentication has no IdP check.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Identity and access management fundamentals”, “Authentication through GitHub.com with additional SAML access restriction”
notes.evidence: If you configure additional SAML access restriction, each person you want to grant access to your enterprise must create and manage a personal account on GitHub.com.

notes.front: With the additional SAML access restriction, which job does the IdP do, and which job stays with the enterprise on GitHub?
notes.back: The IdP authenticates the member; the enterprise grants access to people’s own GitHub.com accounts and does not provision accounts.
notes.explanation: Authentication (proving who you are) is separate from authorization (what you may reach): here the IdP proves identity, and access is granted on GitHub.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Identity and access management fundamentals”, “How does provisioning work?”
notes.evidence: If you use authentication through GitHub.com with additional SAML access restriction, people create personal accounts on GitHub.com, and you can grant those personal accounts access to resources in your enterprise. You do not provision accounts.

notes.front: In an enterprise with personal accounts and SAML SSO, a developer authenticates successfully at the IdP but still cannot see the enterprise’s resources. What is most likely missing?
notes.back: B) Access granted to their personal account in the enterprise
notes.explanation: The IdP proves who the developer is; the enterprise still has to grant access to their GitHub.com account.
notes.choices:
A) A second IdP account
B) Access granted to their personal account in the enterprise
C) A new managed user account
D) An SSH certificate
notes.choicesExplained: A) One IdP account is enough to authenticate. C) Managed user accounts belong to Enterprise Managed Users, not to this enterprise type. D) SSH certificates are for Git access, not for seeing resources.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Identity and access management fundamentals”, “Authentication through GitHub.com with additional SAML access restriction”
notes.evidence: After you grant access to your enterprise, the member can access your enterprise's resources only after authenticating successfully for both the account on GitHub.com and for an account on your SAML identity provider (IdP).

notes.front: With SAML SSO configured, what happens when a member accesses most resources in the organization?
notes.back: GitHub redirects them to the IdP to authenticate; after success, the IdP redirects them back to GitHub.
notes.explanation: Members still sign in to their personal accounts, so the IdP step is added to the normal sign-in.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About SAML for enterprise IAM”, “About SAML SSO for your enterprise”
notes.evidence: If you configure SAML SSO, members of your organization will continue to sign into their personal accounts on GitHub.com. When a member accesses most resources within your organization, GitHub redirects the member to your IdP to authenticate. After successful authentication, your IdP redirects the member back to GitHub.

notes.front: Does SAML SSO replace the normal GitHub sign-in for members with personal accounts?
notes.back: No. Members still sign in to their personal accounts on GitHub.com, and each is linked to an external identity in the IdP.
notes.explanation: Only with Enterprise Managed Users does the IdP account take the place of a personal account.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About SAML for enterprise IAM”, “About SAML SSO for your enterprise”
notes.evidence: SAML SSO does not replace the normal sign-in process for GitHub. Unless you use Enterprise Managed Users, members will continue to sign into their personal accounts on GitHub.com, and each personal account will be linked to an external identity in your IdP.

notes.front: After the enterprise enforces SAML SSO, a developer with a personal account asks whether they can now forget their GitHub.com sign-in and use only the IdP. What is the answer?
notes.back: C) No: they still sign in to their personal account, and SAML SSO adds the IdP step
notes.explanation: Only an enterprise with managed users replaces the personal account; here the personal account is linked to the IdP identity.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: the IdP sign-in replaces the GitHub.com sign-in
B) Yes, but only if 2FA is turned off
C) No: they still sign in to their personal account, and SAML SSO adds the IdP step
D) Only for Git operations on the command line
notes.choicesExplained: A) SAML SSO does not replace GitHub sign-in for personal accounts. B) 2FA has nothing to do with whether the IdP replaces sign-in. D) Git on the command line needs authorized tokens or keys, not an IdP sign-in in place of GitHub.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About SAML for enterprise IAM”, “About SAML SSO for your enterprise”
notes.evidence: SAML SSO does not replace the normal sign-in process for GitHub. Unless you use Enterprise Managed Users, members will continue to sign into their personal accounts on GitHub.com

notes.front: Once SAML SSO is enabled for an enterprise account, who must authenticate through it?
notes.back: All members, to reach the organizations they belong to, and enterprise owners, when accessing the enterprise account.
notes.explanation: The requirement covers both levels: members for their organizations, and owners for the enterprise account itself.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About SAML for enterprise IAM”, “About SAML SSO for your enterprise”
notes.evidence: All members will be required to authenticate using SAML SSO to gain access to the organizations where they are a member, and enterprise owners will be required to authenticate using SAML SSO when accessing an enterprise account.

notes.front: When should an enterprise configure SAML for individual organizations rather than for the enterprise account?
notes.back: When some groups within the enterprise must use different SAML authentication providers.
notes.explanation: One enterprise configuration applies the same provider to every organization, which does not suit groups with different providers.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Deciding whether to configure SAML for your enterprise or your organizations”
notes.evidence: If some groups within your enterprise must use different SAML authentication providers to grant access to your resources on GitHub, configure SAML for individual organizations.

notes.front: If SAML is configured both for the enterprise and for one of its organizations, which configuration applies?
notes.back: The enterprise configuration. It overrides organization configurations, and organizations cannot override it.
notes.explanation: This is what makes enterprise-level SAML a consistent authentication experience across every organization.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Deciding whether to configure SAML for your enterprise or your organizations”
notes.evidence: The SAML configuration for your enterprise overrides any SAML configuration for individual organizations, and organizations cannot override the enterprise configuration.

notes.front: At organization level, what are the two ways to bring in SAML, and what happens to members who miss a deadline?
notes.back: Let users authenticate gradually, or require SAML by a certain date; members who have not authenticated by then are removed.
notes.explanation: The deadline route is firmer: missing it costs organization membership.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Deciding whether to configure SAML for your enterprise or your organizations”
notes.evidence: You can implement SAML for your organizations over time by allowing users to gradually authenticate using SAML, or you can require SAML authentication by a certain date. Organization members who do not authenticate using SAML by this date will be removed.

notes.front: With SAML configured only at organization level, must members authenticate via SAML to access internal repositories?
notes.back: No. Only enterprise-level SAML makes members authenticate before accessing organization resources, including internal repositories.
notes.explanation: So when internal repositories need protecting, GitHub Docs points to configuring SAML for the enterprise account instead.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Deciding whether to configure SAML for your enterprise or your organizations”
notes.evidence: If you configure SAML at the organization level, members are not required to authenticate via SAML to access internal repositories.

notes.front: An enterprise’s three organizations each have their own SAML configuration, all using the same IdP. An audit finds members reaching internal repositories without an IdP sign-in. What fixes this?
notes.back: C) Configure SAML for the enterprise account
notes.explanation: Enterprise SAML protects internal repositories and overrides the organizations’ own configurations; organization-level SAML does not cover them.
notes.choices:
A) Add an SSH certificate authority
B) Require 2FA in each organization
C) Configure SAML for the enterprise account
D) Remove all outside collaborators
notes.choicesExplained: B) 2FA does not make internal repositories need an IdP sign-in. A) An SSH CA governs SSH access to repositories, not IdP authentication. D) Outside collaborators are not the members in question.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Deciding whether to configure SAML for your enterprise or your organizations”
notes.evidence: If you need to protect internal repositories or enforce a consistent authentication experience for every organization in your enterprise, you can configure SAML authentication for your enterprise account instead.

notes.front: After a merger, one organization in an enterprise must keep using its own SAML provider while the others use the parent company’s. Where should SAML be configured?
notes.back: C) For the individual organizations
notes.explanation: Different SAML providers for different groups is the case GitHub Docs gives for organization-level SAML.
notes.choices:
A) For the enterprise account only
B) Nowhere: SAML cannot differ between organizations
C) For the individual organizations
D) For the enterprise account, with an exception for one organization
notes.choicesExplained: A) One enterprise configuration applies to all organizations. B) Organization-level SAML exists for exactly this case. D) Organizations cannot override the enterprise configuration.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Deciding whether to configure SAML for your enterprise or your organizations”
notes.evidence: If some groups within your enterprise must use different SAML authentication providers to grant access to your resources on GitHub, configure SAML for individual organizations.

notes.front: What are the three states SAML SSO can be in for an organization?
notes.back: Disabled; enabled but not enforced; enabled and enforced.
notes.explanation: Enforcing comes last: you can enforce only after enabling SAML SSO and once members have authenticated with the IdP.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About identity and access management with SAML single sign-on”, “About SAML SSO”
notes.evidence: For an organization, SAML SSO can be disabled, enabled but not enforced, or enabled and enforced. After you enable SAML SSO for your organization and your organization's members successfully authenticate with your IdP, you can enforce the SAML SSO configuration.

notes.front: An organization owner has connected the IdP and wants members to start authenticating through it, without anyone losing access yet. Which SAML SSO state fits?
notes.back: D) Enabled but not enforced
notes.explanation: Enforcing is the step taken after members have successfully authenticated with the IdP, so the middle state comes first.
notes.choices:
A) Disabled
B) Enabled and enforced
C) Enforced at enterprise level
D) Enabled but not enforced
notes.choicesExplained: A) Disabled means no one authenticates through the IdP. B) Enforcing should come after members have authenticated successfully. C) Enterprise enforcement applies to every organization, not a trial in one.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About identity and access management with SAML single sign-on”, “About SAML SSO”
notes.evidence: After you enable SAML SSO for your organization and your organization's members successfully authenticate with your IdP, you can enforce the SAML SSO configuration.

notes.front: In an organization with SAML SSO, what are the three ways of accessing a public repository that need no IdP authentication?
notes.back: Viewing its overview page and file contents; forking it; Git read operations such as cloning.
notes.explanation: Other access, such as viewing issues, pull requests, projects and releases, does need IdP authentication.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About identity and access management with SAML single sign-on”, “About SAML SSO”
notes.evidence: IdP authentication is not required for accessing public repositories in certain ways: Viewing the repository's overview page and file contents on GitHub Forking the repository Performing read operations via Git, such as cloning the repository Authentication is required for other access to public repositories, such as viewing issues, pull requests, projects, and releases.

notes.front: In an organization with SAML SSO, must outside collaborators authenticate through SSO?
notes.back: No. SSO authentication is not required for outside collaborators.
notes.explanation: Members, by contrast, are redirected to the IdP when they access most of the organization’s resources.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About identity and access management with SAML single sign-on”, “About SAML SSO”
notes.evidence: SSO authentication is not required for outside collaborators.

notes.front: An organization enforces SAML SSO. A freelance designer, added as an outside collaborator on one repository, has no account in the company’s IdP. What happens when they open that repository?
notes.back: B) They can work there: SSO authentication is not required for outside collaborators
notes.explanation: GitHub Docs exempts outside collaborators from SSO authentication.
notes.choices:
A) They are redirected to the IdP and blocked
B) They can work there: SSO authentication is not required for outside collaborators
C) They must first be given a managed user account
D) They are removed when SAML SSO is enforced
notes.choicesExplained: A) The IdP redirect applies to members, not outside collaborators. C) Managed user accounts belong to Enterprise Managed Users, not to this setup. D) Outside collaborators need no SSO authentication, so enforcing SAML SSO gives no reason to remove them.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About identity and access management with SAML single sign-on”, “About SAML SSO”
notes.evidence: SSO authentication is not required for outside collaborators.

notes.front: How long is the periodic IdP login period for SAML SSO, and what does it achieve?
notes.back: Set by the IdP, generally 24 hours; it limits the length of access and makes users re-identify themselves.
notes.explanation: Members must authenticate with the IdP again periodically to keep reaching the organization’s resources.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About identity and access management with SAML single sign-on”, “About SAML SSO”
notes.evidence: Members must periodically authenticate with your IdP to authenticate and gain access to your organization's resources. The duration of this login period is specified by your IdP and is generally 24 hours. This periodic login requirement limits the length of access and requires users to re-identify themselves to continue.

notes.front: How many external identities can one GitHub account have linked in a given organization?
notes.back: Exactly one; likewise, each external identity links to exactly one GitHub account in an organization.
notes.explanation: The link works both ways, which is why a second GitHub account cannot reuse an identity that is already linked.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About authentication with single sign-on”, “Linked external identities”
notes.evidence: Each GitHub account can be linked to exactly one external identity per organization. Likewise, each external identity can be linked to exactly one GitHub account in an organization.

notes.front: A developer opens a new GitHub account and tries to sign in to the organization’s SSO with their usual IdP identity, which is linked to their old account. They get an error. What must happen?
notes.back: A) An administrator must unlink the external identity from the old account
notes.explanation: Each external identity links to exactly one GitHub account in an organization, so it must be freed before it can be linked again.
notes.choices:
A) An administrator must unlink the external identity from the old account
B) They must create a second IdP identity
C) They must wait for the 24-hour login period to end
D) Nothing: the identity moves automatically
notes.choicesExplained: B) GitHub Docs does not suggest a second identity; the fix is unlinking. C) The login period has nothing to do with the link. D) An identity already linked to another account cannot be used; it does not move by itself.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About authentication with single sign-on”, “Linked external identities”
notes.evidence: If you do want to use that external identity with your GitHub account, you'll need to ask your administrator to unlink your external identity from your old account, so that you can link it to your new account.

notes.front: To use Git on the command line with protected content in an organization that uses SSO, what credential do you need?
notes.back: An authorized personal access token or an authorized SSH key.
notes.explanation: Browser sessions pass through the IdP, but command-line access relies on credentials that have been authorized for the organization.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About authentication with single sign-on”, “Authorizing personal access tokens and SSH keys with SSO”
notes.evidence: To use the API or Git on the command line to access protected content in an organization that uses SSO, you will need to use an authorized personal access token over HTTPS or an authorized SSH key.

notes.front: Before you can authorize a personal access token or SSH key for SSO, what must you have, and how do you get it?
notes.back: A linked external identity, created by authenticating to the organization through the IdP at least once.
notes.explanation: Authorization ties the credential to your identity in that organization, so the identity link must exist first.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Authorizing a personal access token for use with single sign-on”
notes.evidence: Before you can authorize a personal access token or SSH key, you must have a linked external identity. If you're a member of an organization where SSO is enabled, you can create a linked external identity by authenticating to your organization with your identity provider (IdP) at least once.

notes.front: When must a personal access token (classic) be authorized for SSO?
notes.back: After creation, before the token can access an organization that uses SAML SSO.
notes.explanation: A classic token is created first and authorized as a separate step for each such organization.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Authorizing a personal access token for use with single sign-on”
notes.evidence: You must authorize your personal access token (classic) after creation before the token can access an organization that uses SAML single sign-on (SSO).

notes.front: When are fine-grained personal access tokens authorized for SSO?
notes.back: During token creation, before access to the organization is granted.
notes.explanation: Unlike classic tokens, they need no separate authorization step afterwards.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Authorizing a personal access token for use with single sign-on”
notes.evidence: Fine-grained personal access tokens are authorized during token creation, before access to the organization is granted.

notes.front: A developer creates a classic personal access token and a fine-grained one for an organization that enforces SAML SSO. The classic token is refused. Why?
notes.back: B) The classic token has not been authorized for SSO after creation
notes.explanation: Fine-grained tokens are authorized during creation, but a classic token needs a separate authorization after creation.
notes.choices:
A) Classic tokens cannot be used with SSO at all
B) The classic token has not been authorized for SSO after creation
C) Only fine-grained tokens expire
D) The fine-grained token has used up the organization’s allowance
notes.choicesExplained: A) Classic tokens can be used once they are authorized. C) Expiry is not what separates them here. D) There is no such allowance.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Authorizing a personal access token for use with single sign-on”
notes.evidence: You must authorize your personal access token (classic) after creation before the token can access an organization that uses SAML single sign-on (SSO).

notes.front: If you have a linked identity for an organization but it does not enforce SSO, can you use unauthorized tokens and SSH keys with it?
notes.back: No. With a linked identity you can use only authorized tokens and SSH keys with that organization, even if SSO is not enforced.
notes.explanation: You have a linked identity once you have authenticated via SSO for the organization, unless an owner later revoked it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Authorizing a personal access token for use with single sign-on”
notes.evidence: If you have a linked identity for an organization, you can only use authorized personal access tokens and SSH keys with that organization, even if SSO is not enforced. You have a linked identity for an organization if you've ever authenticated via SSO for that organization, unless an organization or enterprise owner later revoked the linked identity.

notes.front: An authorized token stays authorized until it is revoked. What are two ways that can happen?
notes.back: Among others: an organization or enterprise owner revokes the authorization, or you are removed from the organization.
notes.explanation: Editing a token’s scopes, regenerating it or letting it expire also ends the authorization.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Authorizing a personal access token for use with single sign-on”
notes.evidence: After you authorize a personal access token or SSH key, the token or key will stay authorized until revoked in one of the following ways. An organization or enterprise owner revokes the authorization.

notes.front: What does access to SSO-protected internal resources in an enterprise require?
notes.back: An SSO session for any organization in the enterprise.
notes.explanation: This lets code and work be shared across organizations in the enterprise without users joining each organization.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About authentication with single sign-on”, “About authentication with SSO”
notes.evidence: Access to SSO protected internal resources in an enterprise, such as repositories, projects, and packages, requires an SSO session for any organization in the enterprise. This allows code and work to be shared across organizations in an enterprise without requiring users to join each organization.

notes.front: After an owner enables or enforces SSO for an organization and you first authenticate via SSO, what must you do about apps you had already authorized for it?
notes.back: Reauthorize any OAuth apps or GitHub Apps you previously authorized to access the organization.
notes.explanation: Each app authorization also needs an active SSO session, so earlier authorizations have to be renewed through SSO.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About authentication with single sign-on”, “About OAuth apps, GitHub Apps, and SSO”
notes.evidence: After an enterprise or organization owner enables or enforces SSO for an organization, and after you authenticate via SSO for the first time, you must reauthorize any OAuth apps or GitHub Apps that you previously authorized to access the organization.

notes.front: What support does GitHub give for SAML SSO with an IdP that is not on its tested list?
notes.back: Limited support, for any identity provider that implements the SAML 2.0 standard.
notes.explanation: Full support is for the IdPs GitHub tests and officially supports; others get limited support if they follow SAML 2.0.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About SAML for enterprise IAM”, “Supported IdPs”
notes.evidence: We test and officially support the following IdPs. For SAML SSO, we offer limited support for all identity providers that implement the SAML 2.0 standard.

notes.front: Which on-premises Microsoft federation product is on GitHub’s list of officially supported SAML IdPs?
notes.back: Microsoft Active Directory Federation Services.
notes.explanation: It is one of six IdPs GitHub officially supports and internally tests for SAML.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About identity and access management with SAML single sign-on”, “Supported SAML services”
notes.evidence: GitHub officially supports and internally tests the following IdPs for SAML. Microsoft Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS)

notes.front: Which Microsoft cloud identity service is on GitHub’s list of officially supported SAML IdPs?
notes.back: Microsoft Entra ID.
notes.explanation: GitHub Docs notes that the service was previously known under an older Azure name.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About identity and access management with SAML single sign-on”, “Supported SAML services”
notes.evidence: Microsoft Entra ID (previously known as Azure AD)

notes.front: Which Ping product is on GitHub’s list of officially supported SAML IdPs?
notes.back: PingOne.
notes.explanation: It sits on the same tested list as Okta, OneLogin and Shibboleth.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About identity and access management with SAML single sign-on”, “Supported SAML services”
notes.evidence: Okta OneLogin PingOne Shibboleth

notes.front: A university uses an identity provider that is not on GitHub’s tested list but implements the SAML 2.0 standard. What can it expect for SAML SSO?
notes.back: C) Limited support from GitHub
notes.explanation: GitHub tests and officially supports a named list; other IdPs still work if they follow SAML 2.0, with a lower level of support.
notes.choices:
A) Full official support, as for any IdP
B) No SAML SSO at all
C) Limited support from GitHub
D) Support only through OpenID Connect
notes.choicesExplained: A) Full official support is for tested IdPs only. B) SAML 2.0 IdPs can be used. D) OpenID Connect is for Enterprise Managed Users with Entra ID, not a fallback for other IdPs.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About SAML for enterprise IAM”, “Supported IdPs”
notes.evidence: For SAML SSO, we offer limited support for all identity providers that implement the SAML 2.0 standard.

notes.front: If you did not save the enterprise’s single sign-on recovery codes when configuring SSO, can you still get them?
notes.back: Yes, from the enterprise’s settings.
notes.explanation: GitHub Docs says you should download them so you can reach GitHub if the IdP is unavailable.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Downloading your enterprise account’s single sign-on recovery codes”
notes.evidence: If you did not save your recovery codes when you configured SSO, you can still access the codes from your enterprise's settings.

notes.front: The company’s IdP suffers a long outage, and an enterprise owner urgently needs to change an enterprise setting on GitHub. What should they use?
notes.back: D) One of the enterprise’s single sign-on recovery codes
notes.explanation: Single sign-on recovery codes exist for signing in to the enterprise when the IdP is unavailable.
notes.choices:
A) A personal access token
B) A 2FA recovery code for their own account
C) An SSH certificate
D) One of the enterprise’s single sign-on recovery codes
notes.choicesExplained: A) Tokens are for Git and programmatic access, not for signing in to the enterprise. B) Personal 2FA recovery codes restore a personal account’s 2FA, not access past an unavailable IdP. C) SSH certificates are for Git over SSH.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Downloading your enterprise account’s single sign-on recovery codes”
notes.evidence: In the event that your IdP is unavailable, you can use a recovery code to sign in and access your enterprise on GitHub.

notes.front: For Enterprise Managed Users, which IdP supports OIDC and CAP?
notes.back: Only Microsoft Entra ID.
notes.explanation: Enterprises with other IdPs use SAML for authentication instead.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring OIDC for Enterprise Managed Users”
notes.evidence: OpenID Connect (OIDC) and Conditional Access Policy (CAP) support for Enterprise Managed Users is only available for Microsoft Entra ID (previously known as Azure AD).

notes.front: An enterprise with managed users authenticates through Okta and wants GitHub to enforce its IdP’s conditional access rules through OIDC. What should the administrator know?
notes.back: B) OIDC and CAP support for Enterprise Managed Users is only available with Microsoft Entra ID
notes.explanation: The Entra ID restriction applies to both OIDC and CAP support for Enterprise Managed Users.
notes.choices:
A) It works once OIDC is enabled in Okta
B) OIDC and CAP support for Enterprise Managed Users is only available with Microsoft Entra ID
C) CAP works with any SAML IdP
D) CAP needs GitHub Connect
notes.choicesExplained: A) OIDC support for Enterprise Managed Users is not available with Okta. C) CAP support comes with OIDC, not with SAML. D) GitHub Connect is a GHES feature.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring OIDC for Enterprise Managed Users”
notes.evidence: OpenID Connect (OIDC) and Conditional Access Policy (CAP) support for Enterprise Managed Users is only available for Microsoft Entra ID (previously known as Azure AD).

notes.front: How many OIDC integrations with Enterprise Managed Users can one Entra ID tenant support?
notes.back: One. To connect Entra ID to more than one enterprise on GitHub, use SAML instead.
notes.explanation: The one-integration limit is per tenant, so a second enterprise needs the SAML route.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring OIDC for Enterprise Managed Users”, “Identity provider support”
notes.evidence: Each Entra ID tenant can support only one OIDC integration with Enterprise Managed Users. If you want to connect Entra ID to more than one enterprise on GitHub, use SAML instead.

notes.front: A group runs two enterprises with managed users and wants both connected to the same Entra ID tenant. How should they authenticate?
notes.back: A) SAML, because one tenant supports only one OIDC integration
notes.explanation: GitHub Docs says to use SAML when connecting Entra ID to more than one enterprise.
notes.choices:
A) SAML, because one tenant supports only one OIDC integration
B) OIDC for both enterprises
C) OIDC for one and CAP for the other
D) Neither: one tenant can serve only one enterprise
notes.choicesExplained: B) A tenant supports only one OIDC integration. C) CAP is not an authentication method on its own; it comes with OIDC. D) With SAML, one Entra ID tenant can connect to more than one enterprise.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring OIDC for Enterprise Managed Users”, “Identity provider support”
notes.evidence: If you want to connect Entra ID to more than one enterprise on GitHub, use SAML instead.

notes.front: An enterprise with managed users uses SAML SSO but wants CAP support. What path does GitHub Docs offer?
notes.back: A migration path from SAML to OIDC.
notes.explanation: CAP support comes with OIDC, so a SAML enterprise has to move to OIDC to benefit from it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring OIDC for Enterprise Managed Users”, “About OIDC for Enterprise Managed Users”
notes.evidence: If you currently use SAML SSO for authentication and would prefer to use OIDC and benefit from CAP support, you can follow a migration path.

notes.front: An enterprise uses OIDC with Entra ID, and its CAP allows only the office network. A developer uses their token from a café. What happens?
notes.back: A) GitHub checks the CAP IP conditions for the token’s authentication, so access is refused
notes.explanation: With OIDC SSO, GitHub validates each authentication with a token or SSH key tied to a user account against the CAP IP conditions.
notes.choices:
A) GitHub checks the CAP IP conditions for the token’s authentication, so access is refused
B) The token works, because CAP applies only to SSH keys
C) The token works, because CAP applies only to the web interface
D) The developer is removed from the enterprise
notes.choicesExplained: C) CAP also covers authentication with tokens and SSH keys. B) Tokens are covered as well as SSH keys. D) A failed condition blocks the interaction; it does not remove anyone.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring OIDC for Enterprise Managed Users”, “About OIDC for Enterprise Managed Users”
notes.evidence: GitHub will automatically use your IdP's conditional access policy (CAP) IP conditions to validate interactions with GitHub when members use the web UI or change IP addresses, and for each authentication with a personal access token or SSH key associated with a user account.

notes.front: Do managed user accounts have a password or 2FA methods stored on GitHub?
notes.back: No. They authenticate only through the IdP.
notes.explanation: As a result, managed users do not see the sudo prompt when taking sensitive actions.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities and restrictions of managed user accounts”, “Authentication”
notes.evidence: Managed user accounts authenticate using only your identity provider, and have no password or two-factor authentication methods stored on GitHub. As a result, they do not see the sudo prompt when taking sensitive actions.

notes.front: An administrator of an enterprise with managed users looks for the enterprise policy that requires 2FA for all organizations. What will they find?
notes.back: C) It is not available for enterprises with managed users
notes.explanation: Managed users authenticate only through the IdP and keep no 2FA methods on GitHub, and the enterprise 2FA policy is not offered for them.
notes.choices:
A) It is available and applies to managed users like any other
B) It applies only to outside collaborators
C) It is not available for enterprises with managed users
D) It must be set in each organization instead
notes.choicesExplained: A) GitHub Docs says the policy is not available for this enterprise type. B) The policy is simply not offered here. D) Moving the setting to organizations does not change that managed users keep no 2FA on GitHub.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for security settings in your enterprise”, “Requiring two-factor authentication for organizations in your enterprise”
notes.evidence: Enterprise owners can require that organization members, billing managers, and outside collaborators in all organizations owned by an enterprise use two-factor authentication to secure their user accounts. This policy is not available for enterprises with managed users.

notes.front: In an enterprise with managed users, what does an unauthenticated visitor see by default, and why?
notes.back: A 404 error, which hides the existence of private resources.
notes.explanation: Administrators can instead turn on automatic redirects to SSO through the IdP.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for security settings in your enterprise”, “Managing SSO for unauthenticated users”
notes.evidence: By default, to hide the existence of private resources, when an unauthenticated user attempts to access your enterprise, GitHub displays a 404 error.

notes.front: When an organization requires 2FA, what happens to members and billing managers who do not use it?
notes.back: They cannot access the organization’s resources until they enable 2FA, but keep their membership, still consuming seats.
notes.explanation: Unlike outside collaborators, members are not removed, so their seats keep counting.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Requiring two-factor authentication in your organization”, “About two-factor authentication for organizations”
notes.evidence: When you require use of two-factor authentication for your organization, members and billing managers who do not use 2FA will not be able to access your organization's resources until they enable 2FA on their account. They will retain membership even without 2FA, including consuming seats in your organization.

notes.front: When an organization requires 2FA, what happens to outside collaborators who do not use it?
notes.back: They are removed from the organization, losing access to its repositories and to their forks of its private repositories.
notes.explanation: Their access can be reinstated if they enable 2FA within three months of removal.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Requiring two-factor authentication in your organization”, “About two-factor authentication for organizations”
notes.evidence: When you require use of two-factor authentication for your organization, outside collaborators who do not use 2FA will be removed from the organization and lose access to its repositories. They will also lose access to their forks of the organization's private repositories.

notes.front: After an organization requires 2FA, what happens to bots and service accounts that are outside collaborators without 2FA?
notes.back: They are removed from the organization and lose access to its repositories.
notes.explanation: Unattended or shared accounts are treated like any outside collaborator, so their 2FA has to be configured too.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Requiring two-factor authentication in your organization”, “About two-factor authentication for organizations”
notes.evidence: You will also need to enable two-factor authentication for unattended or shared access accounts that are outside collaborators, such as bots and service accounts. If you do not configure 2FA for these unattended outside collaborator accounts after you've enabled required 2FA, the accounts will be removed from the organization and lose access to their repositories.

notes.front: An organization turns on required 2FA. Neither a member nor an outside collaborator has 2FA. What happens to each?
notes.back: B) The member loses access but stays a member; the outside collaborator is removed
notes.explanation: Members keep membership and seats without access, while outside collaborators without 2FA are removed.
notes.choices:
A) Both are removed
B) The member loses access but stays a member; the outside collaborator is removed
C) Both stay and keep access until they next sign in
D) The member is removed; the outside collaborator only loses access
notes.choicesExplained: A) Members are not removed; they keep membership and seats. C) Access is lost straight away, not at next sign-in. D) This reverses what happens to each.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Requiring two-factor authentication in your organization”, “About two-factor authentication for organizations”
notes.evidence: members and billing managers who do not use 2FA will not be able to access your organization's resources until they enable 2FA on their account. They will retain membership even without 2FA, including consuming seats in your organization.

notes.front: What must an organization owner do before they can require 2FA for members, outside collaborators and billing managers?
notes.back: Enable 2FA on their own account.
notes.explanation: GitHub Docs also recommends notifying people and asking them to set up 2FA first.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Requiring two-factor authentication in your organization”, “Prerequisites”
notes.evidence: Before you can require organization members, outside collaborators, and billing managers to use two-factor authentication, you must enable 2FA for your account.

notes.front: A newly appointed organization owner, who has never set up 2FA, tries to require 2FA for everyone on their first day. What must happen first?
notes.back: B) The owner enables 2FA on their own account
notes.explanation: Enabling 2FA on your own account is the stated prerequisite for requiring it of others.
notes.choices:
A) Every member enables 2FA
B) The owner enables 2FA on their own account
C) The enterprise turns on SAML SSO
D) GitHub Support approves the change
notes.choicesExplained: A) Members are asked, not required, to set up 2FA first; the hard prerequisite is the owner’s own. C) SAML SSO is not a prerequisite. D) No approval from GitHub Support is needed.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Requiring two-factor authentication in your organization”, “Prerequisites”
notes.evidence: Before you can require organization members, outside collaborators, and billing managers to use two-factor authentication, you must enable 2FA for your account.

notes.front: When an organization requires secure two-factor methods, who is prevented from accessing its resources?
notes.back: Users with no secure 2FA method configured, and users who have any insecure method, such as SMS, configured.
notes.explanation: Having a secure method is not enough; an insecure one left configured also blocks access.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Requiring two-factor authentication in your organization”, “Requiring secure methods of two-factor authentication in your organization”
notes.evidence: Users who do not have a secure method of 2FA configured, or who have any insecure method (such as SMS) configured, will be prevented from accessing organization resources.

notes.front: An organization requires secure two-factor methods. A member uses an authenticator app but also keeps text-message codes as a backup. What happens?
notes.back: D) They lose access to organization resources until they remove the insecure method
notes.explanation: Users with any insecure method, such as SMS, configured are prevented from accessing organization resources.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: the authenticator app is enough
B) They are removed from the organization
C) They are moved to the outside collaborator role
D) They lose access to organization resources until they remove the insecure method
notes.choicesExplained: A) Any insecure method configured blocks access, even alongside a secure one. B) The secure-methods requirement prevents access; it does not remove members. C) Roles do not change.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Requiring two-factor authentication in your organization”, “Requiring secure methods of two-factor authentication in your organization”
notes.evidence: Users who do not have a secure method of 2FA configured, or who have any insecure method (such as SMS) configured, will be prevented from accessing organization resources.

notes.front: Whom can enterprise owners require to use 2FA across the enterprise, and for which enterprise type is this policy unavailable?
notes.back: Organization members, billing managers and outside collaborators in all its organizations; unavailable for enterprises with managed users.
notes.explanation: It sets the organization-level requirement for every organization at once, but managed users keep no 2FA on GitHub.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for security settings in your enterprise”, “Requiring two-factor authentication for organizations in your enterprise”
notes.evidence: Enterprise owners can require that organization members, billing managers, and outside collaborators in all organizations owned by an enterprise use two-factor authentication to secure their user accounts. This policy is not available for enterprises with managed users.

notes.front: What are two actions that make an account eligible for mandatory 2FA?
notes.back: Among others: publishing an app or action for others; creating a release for your repository.
notes.explanation: Each shows that the account is a contributor; being an organization owner or enterprise administrator also counts.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About mandatory two-factor authentication”, “About eligibility for mandatory 2FA”
notes.evidence: Eligible actions include: Publishing an app or action for others Creating a release for your repository Contributing to specific high-importance repositories

notes.front: Which users are not required to enable 2FA under GitHub’s mandatory 2FA?
notes.back: Enterprise Managed Users and on-premises GitHub Enterprise Server users; it applies only to users with a password on GitHub.com.
notes.explanation: Neither kind of account signs in with a GitHub.com password, which is what the programme covers.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About mandatory two-factor authentication”, “About mandatory 2FA for organizations and enterprises”
notes.evidence: GitHub Enterprise Managed Users and on-premise GitHub Enterprise Server users are not required to enable 2FA. Mandatory 2FA enablement only applies to users with a password on GitHub.com.

notes.front: Which of these people can GitHub’s mandatory 2FA programme apply to?
notes.back: C) A GitHub.com personal account holder who publishes releases
notes.explanation: Mandatory 2FA applies only to users with a password on GitHub.com, and creating a release is an eligible action.
notes.choices:
A) A managed user account holder in an enterprise with managed users
B) A developer on the company’s on-premises GHES instance
C) A GitHub.com personal account holder who publishes releases
D) None of them: only organizations can require 2FA
notes.choicesExplained: A) Managed users are not required to enable 2FA. B) On-premises GHES users are not required either. D) GitHub runs its own mandatory programme, separate from organization requirements.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About mandatory two-factor authentication”, “About mandatory 2FA for organizations and enterprises”
notes.evidence: GitHub Enterprise Managed Users and on-premise GitHub Enterprise Server users are not required to enable 2FA. Mandatory 2FA enablement only applies to users with a password on GitHub.com.

notes.front: How does GitHub’s mandatory 2FA relate to an organization’s or enterprise’s own 2FA requirement?
notes.back: They are separate: mandatory 2FA is required by GitHub itself; an administrator’s requirement is a condition of joining their organization or enterprise.
notes.explanation: Being selected by GitHub does not change how an owner turns on the organization’s requirement, and the reverse holds too.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About mandatory two-factor authentication”, “About mandatory 2FA for organizations and enterprises”
notes.evidence: Mandatory 2FA is required by GitHub itself to improve security for both individual developers and the broader software development ecosystem. Your administrator may also require 2FA enablement as a requirement to join their organization or enterprise, but those requirements are separate from this program.

notes.front: If a user selected for mandatory 2FA already signs in through corporate SSO with 2FA, must they still enrol in 2FA on GitHub.com?
notes.back: Yes. SSO with 2FA protects organization and enterprise resources, but not user-owned content on GitHub.com unrelated to them.
notes.explanation: GitHub Docs adds that SSO with 2FA does not protect a user’s profile and settings either.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About mandatory two-factor authentication”, “About SAML SSO and mandatory 2FA”
notes.evidence: you must enroll in 2FA on GitHub.com even if your company already requires single sign-on (SSO) with 2FA. While SSO with 2FA is a powerful way to protect organization or enterprise-owned resources, it does not protect user-owned content on GitHub.com unrelated to an organization or enterprise

notes.front: Under mandatory 2FA, how long are the setup period and the grace period, and what happens after both expire?
notes.back: 45 days to set up, then a 7-day grace period; after that you cannot access GitHub.com until you enable 2FA.
notes.explanation: Trying to use GitHub.com after that point prompts you to enable 2FA.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About mandatory two-factor authentication”, “About failure to enable mandatory 2FA”
notes.evidence: If you do not enable 2FA within the 45 day setup period, and you allow the 7 day grace period to expire, you will not be able to access GitHub.com until you enable 2FA. If you attempt to access GitHub.com, you will be prompted to enable 2FA.

notes.front: Can members use the enterprise’s SSH certificates to access user-owned repositories?
notes.back: Only if the enterprise uses managed user accounts, where it can be enabled; with personal accounts it cannot.
notes.explanation: Managed user accounts belong to the enterprise, so it can extend certificate access to their own repositories.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for security settings in your enterprise”, “Managing access to user-owned repositories”
notes.evidence: You can enable or disable access to user-owned repositories with an SSH certificate if your enterprise uses managed user accounts. However, if your enterprise uses personal accounts on GitHub.com members cannot use the certificate to access personally-owned repositories.

notes.front: When you issue each SSH client certificate, what must it include?
notes.back: An extension that specifies which GitHub user the certificate is for.
notes.explanation: GitHub validates the certificate’s signature and fields, including its validity period, against the trusted CA.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for security settings in your enterprise”, “Managing SSH certificate authorities for your enterprise”
notes.evidence: GitHub uses OpenSSH-format SSH user certificates to authenticate Git operations over SSH by validating the certificate's signature and fields (including its validity period) against a trusted SSH certificate authority (CA) configured at the organization and/or enterprise level. When you issue each client certificate, you must include an extension that specifies which GitHub user the certificate is for.

notes.front: Can the same SSH certificate authority be uploaded to two organizations on GitHub?
notes.back: No. Each certificate authority can be uploaded to only one account on GitHub.
notes.explanation: Once a CA is added to an organization or enterprise, it cannot be added to another organization or enterprise account.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for security settings in your enterprise”, “Adding an SSH certificate authority”
notes.evidence: Each certificate authority can only be uploaded to one account on GitHub. If an SSH certificate authority has been added to an organization or enterprise account, you cannot add the same certificate authority to another organization or enterprise account on GitHub.

notes.front: An enterprise has uploaded CA one; one of its organizations has uploaded CA two. Which certificates can reach that organization’s repositories?
notes.back: A) Certificates from either CA
notes.explanation: With one CA on the enterprise and another on an organization in it, either can be used for that organization’s repositories.
notes.choices:
A) Certificates from either CA
B) Only those from CA two, because the organization is closer
C) Neither, because two CAs conflict
D) Only those from CA one, because the enterprise overrides
notes.choicesExplained: D) and B) Neither CA overrides the other for this organization. C) The two CAs do not conflict.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for security settings in your enterprise”, “Adding an SSH certificate authority”
notes.evidence: If you add one certificate authority to an enterprise and another certificate authority to an organization in the enterprise, either certificate authority can be used to access the organization's repositories.

notes.front: When an organization requires SSH certificates, which ways of authenticating to its repositories stop working?
notes.back: HTTPS, and SSH with an unsigned key, even one authorized for an organization that uses SSO.
notes.explanation: Authorized GitHub Apps, deploy keys and features such as GitHub Actions and Codespaces are exempt.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for security settings in your enterprise”, “Adding an SSH certificate authority”
notes.evidence: When you require SSH certificates, users will not be able to authenticate to access the organization's repositories over HTTPS or with an unsigned SSH key, regardless of whether the SSH key is authorized for an organization that requires authentication through an external identity system.

notes.front: An organization now requires SSH certificates. A developer’s ordinary SSH key, authorized for SSO months ago, is refused. What must the developer use?
notes.back: D) A certificate signed by the organization’s trusted CA
notes.explanation: Requiring certificates blocks HTTPS and unsigned keys, whether or not they are authorized for SSO.
notes.choices:
A) A classic personal access token over HTTPS
B) The same key, authorized for SSO again
C) A new unsigned SSH key
D) A certificate signed by the organization’s trusted CA
notes.choicesExplained: B) SSO authorization does not help an unsigned key once certificates are required. C) Any unsigned key is refused. A) HTTPS access is refused too.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for security settings in your enterprise”, “Adding an SSH certificate authority”
notes.evidence: When you require SSH certificates, users will not be able to authenticate to access the organization's repositories over HTTPS or with an unsigned SSH key, regardless of whether the SSH key is authorized for an organization that requires authentication through an external identity system.

notes.front: What happens to certificates when you delete an SSH certificate authority from the enterprise?
notes.back: GitHub immediately stops accepting certificates signed by that CA, including ones not yet expired.
notes.explanation: Deletion cannot be undone; trusting the CA again means uploading its public key again.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for security settings in your enterprise”, “Deleting an SSH certificate authority”
notes.evidence: Deleting a CA immediately prevents GitHub from accepting SSH certificates signed by that CA, including certificates that have not yet expired.
